title: God's church in the last days
summary: Prophecy does not only describe the powers hostile to God - it also shows where His faithful people are in the last days: the remnant, who keep the commandments, hold the testimony of Jesus and have the gift of prophecy, and whose distinguishing mark is a global mission of proclaiming Christ's return.

sections.heading: Does prophecy point to a faithful people?

items.comment: After the account of persecution, the dragon goes after the *rest* of her offspring - those who "keep God's commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus." Prophecy points to a faithful people at the very end of history.

questions.text: Why does it matter that God has a recognizable people even in the time of great tribulation?

items.comment: After the message of the three angels, the same portrait appears: "the saints, who keep God's commandments and the faith of Jesus." Two marks return like a refrain.

questions.text: What does it mean that obedience and faith in Jesus always go together here, never apart?

items.label: "the remnant/rest" (Rev 12:17)
items.content: The Greek term rendered "rest / remaining ones" (loipoi) describes the final part of the offspring of the "woman" (the church), against whom the dragon strikes. The biblical motif of the remnant (cf. Isa 10:20-22; Rom 11:5) does not mean an elite of better people, but a faithful group preserved by God through a time of testing. The two defining marks in Rev 12:17 - they "keep God's commandments" and "hold the testimony of Jesus" - return in Rev 14:12 and 19:10. The Greek form has been deliberately omitted here as uncertain - to be confirmed at review.

items.label: "the remnant" across the whole Bible: three meanings
items.content: The term "rest / remnant" runs from Genesis to Revelation, and in the Old Testament alone it appears more than 540 times. Bible scholars distinguish three shades of meaning: (1) the historical remnant - those who survived a catastrophe; (2) the faithful remnant - those who in a given generation remain in covenant with God; (3) the eschatological remnant - believers who keep the faith to the very end of the church's history. The "remnant of the last days" in Revelation is this third shade - not a new elite, but the fulfillment of that same story of faithfulness.

items.comment: John sets out a simple test: we know God if we "keep His commandments." Obedience is not the price of the relationship, but its evidence.

questions.text: How can you tell obedience born of love from obedience born of fear or calculation?

items.comment: Jesus puts it in a single sentence: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments." First love, then - as its fruit - obedience.

questions.text: What changes when the order is reversed: not "obey in order to be loved," but "you love, so you obey"?

items.label: "to fear God" as loving obedience
items.content: The Hebrew idea of "fearing God" (cf. Deut 10:12-13; Eccl 12:13), which returns in the message of the first angel ("fear God," Rev 14:7), does not mean dread of punishment, but reverent trust expressed in obedience born of love. Moses links this "fear" with clinging to God after His act of deliverance from Egypt - first grace and rescue, then grateful obedience. It is the same order Jesus captures in John 14:15: love gives rise to obedience, not the other way around.

sections.heading: Distinguishing marks: the commandments and the gift of prophecy

items.comment: The "testimony of Jesus" is not vague - Revelation will define it shortly. Together with "the commandments" it forms the twofold mark of God's people in the last days.

questions.text: What can you expect from a community that truly "holds the testimony of Jesus"?

items.comment: The angel explains: "the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy." The gift of prophecy becomes a mark of the remnant - a sign, not an ornament.

questions.text: What does it say about God's care that in the last days He sends His people the gift of prophecy?

items.label: "the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy" (Rev 19:10)
items.content: Rev 19:10 identifies "the testimony of Jesus" with "the spirit of prophecy." Adventism understands this as a promise of an active prophetic gift in the remnant church (cf. Joel 2:28; Rev 12:17). An important balance must be kept here, without any pressure: the ministry of Ellen White is sometimes regarded as a modern expression of this gift, yet the foundation and ultimate test remains Scripture alone (Isa 8:20; 1 Thess 5:21) - sola scriptura. No gift stands ABOVE Scripture or ALONGSIDE it as a second norm; the gift serves to point back to the Word. This interpretation should be presented as an encouragement, not as a condition of belonging - to be discussed with the reviewer.

items.label: "those who have the testimony of Jesus" are prophets (Rev 19:10; 22:9)
items.content: The angel first calls John a fellow servant of those "who have the testimony of Jesus" (Rev 19:10), and later repeats an almost identical sentence as a fellow servant of "the prophets, your brothers" (Rev 22:9). Setting these two passages side by side shows that "those who have the testimony of Jesus" are the ones through whom the prophetic gift works. This is not a decorative metaphor, but a concrete promise that God will guide His people through prophetic gifting - always subject to Scripture.

items.comment: Joel already foretold that "in the last days" God would pour out His Spirit, and "your sons and daughters will prophesy." The gift of prophecy in the last days is foretold, not invented.

questions.text: How can this gift help a community stay faithful to Scripture rather than drift away from it?

items.label: Joel's promise: the "early" and "latter rain"
items.content: On the day of Pentecost, Peter declared that Joel's prophecy (Joel 2:28-32) was fulfilled in the outpouring of the Spirit on the newborn church (Acts 2:16-21). Yet this initial fulfillment - a picture of the "early rain" - does not exhaust the prophecy. Revelation points to its full, global completion at the close of the church's history, when the Spirit will be poured out on the remnant across the whole world (Rev 18:1). The same gift that brought the apostolic church to life is meant to prepare God's people once more for the return of Jesus.

items.comment: Revelation ends with a blessing for the one "who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book." God's people read the prophecies and obey them - this is readiness, not curiosity.

questions.text: What does it practically mean to "keep" the words of prophecy, and not merely to "know" them?

items.comment: Paul balances two extremes: "do not despise prophecies," and at the same time "test everything." The gift of prophecy does not replace the Bible - it is subject to it.

questions.text: How do you keep the balance: not despising the gift of prophecy, yet testing everything by Scripture?

items.comment: The unchanging measure of every prophecy: "to the Law and to the testimony!" - if anyone speaks otherwise, they have no light. The Bible remains the foundation and the test.

questions.text: Why must every gift and every teacher be tested by Scripture, and not the other way around?

items.label: "the word of God" and "the testimony of Jesus" - the axis of Revelation
items.content: The pairing of "the word of God" and "the testimony of Jesus" recurs throughout Revelation like a leading theme (Rev 1:2, 9; 6:9; 12:17; 20:4). Scholars see in it the line that separates the faithful from the unfaithful - it was loyalty to these two things that brought persecution on the disciples, including the exile of John himself. These same two marks define the remnant (Rev 12:17): to hold fast to the Word and to have the testimony of Jesus. They are not two competing norms - the testimony always points back to the Word.

sections.heading: A people with a mission to the whole world

items.comment: The first angel carries the eternal gospel "to every nation, tribe, language and people." God's people in the last days have a global reach - no one is left out.

questions.text: What does it mean that the message is to reach "every" nation - even where it is hard?

items.label: the three angels: one threefold message
items.content: The messages of the three angels (Rev 14:6-12) are not three separate proclamations, but blend into one threefold call. At the heart of the first is the "eternal gospel" and the summons to "fear God (...) and worship the Creator"; the second announces the fall of Babylon; the third warns against the mark of the beast. All three sound within one window of time - between 1844 and the return of Christ - because right after the third angel comes the harvest of the earth (Rev 14:14-16). This is heaven's last loving call to humanity.

items.label: "worship the Creator": the first angel and creation
items.content: The first angel's call to worship the One "who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water" (Rev 14:7) draws directly, in its wording, on the fourth commandment (Ex 20:8-11) and on the account of creation (Gen 2:1-3). The message of the last days is therefore positive: it does not so much criticize as invite everyone back to worship of the Creator. The "hour of judgment" here is tied to the beginning of the judgment of Dan 7:9-10 - this call turns our gaze toward God, not toward fear.

items.comment: Jesus ties the end to mission: "this gospel will be preached throughout the whole earth (...) and then the end will come." Proclaiming the return of Jesus is a distinguishing mark of this people.

questions.text: How does the meaning of your life change if you belong to a people with the mission to "prepare the world for the return of Jesus"?

items.comment: The mission also has the tone of an invitation: "Come out of her, my people." God calls His own out of "Babylon" not by force, but by a call of love - without aggression.

questions.text: How can we proclaim truth firmly, yet with a love that invites rather than repels?

items.label: "Babylon": a system, not people
items.content: The Babylon of Revelation is an image woven from prophecies about ancient Babylon (see Isa 21:9; Jer 51:6-7) - the power that once oppressed God's people and profaned His temple. In Revelation, however, it has no ethnic or geographic boundaries: it stands for religion mixed with error, a false system of worship, not particular people or nations. That is why we speak of ideas and systems, never in a tone of attack on individuals. The very name "Babel" is linked to mixture and confusion (cf. Gen 11:9).

items.label: "come out of her, my people": God's people are in Babylon
items.content: The very call to "come out of her, my people" (Rev 18:4) assumes something moving: in "Babylon" there are still people who belong to God. This is therefore not a condemnation, but a call of love - an invitation to come out before the last plagues fall. It is worth stressing that God "has His children" who have not yet come to know the fullness of truth; the remnant is therefore not a circle of the chosen who stand above others, but a community with a mission to invite. This rules out all triumphalism and any sense of superiority.

items.comment: The identity of God's people is positive: "a chosen people (...), to proclaim the praises of the One who called you." We are not defined by what we are against, but by the One to whom we belong.

questions.text: What does it mean to define your community by "whose we are" rather than by "whom we are against"?

items.comment: At the core of the message is a positive call: "worship the Creator." God's people do not so much criticize others as invite everyone back to the Creator.

questions.text: If someone from the outside looked at your community, would they see criticism first, or an invitation to God?

items.label: "to which church?": marks, not labels
items.content: The question "where are God's people today?" is settled by prophecy through MARKS, not by a denominational name: (1) faithfulness to all of God's commandments, (2) living faith and the testimony of Jesus, (3) the presence of the gift of prophecy, (4) a global mission of proclaiming the eternal gospel and the return of Christ (Rev 14:6-12; Matt 24:14). Pointing to these marks is an invitation, not a condemnation of other Christians - God has "His people" outside the visible structures as well (Rev 18:4) and is calling them to Himself. The tone: without aggression, with respect, sola scriptura.

application.text: Prophecy does not leave the question "where are God's people today?" unanswered - but it answers through marks, not through boasting. You recognize the faithful people of the last days by this: they hold fast to all of God's commandments, live by the faith of Jesus, treasure the gift of prophecy under the authority of the Bible, and carry to the world one piece of good news: Jesus is coming back. This is no cause for a sense of superiority, but for humility and responsibility. It is not about a label on the door, but about whether my life and my community bear these marks - and whether our first word to the world is an invitation to the Creator, not an attack.
application.challenge: Hold the four prophetic marks of God's people (the commandments, faith in / the testimony of Jesus, the gift of prophecy under the authority of Scripture, mission) up against your own life and community - where do you want to grow? Name one person too, to whom this week, with love and without pressure, you will share the hope of Jesus' return.
